back: A temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service or result.
Unique; definite objectives; needs resources; fixed time frame (start and finish); risk and uncertainty; cross-functional team.
Scope, time and cost: Performance $= f(S, C, T)$. Change one and the others change.
Conceptualisation → Planning (DPR) → Execution → Termination.
S: slow start, fast middle, slow finish (watershed). J: slow start, then ever faster (energy plantation).
Industrial: limited scale, private promoters, judged by IRR, market finance repaid in 7–10 years. Development: large, government/NGO, judged by ERR, soft loans up to 25+ years.
Opportunity/support studies → identify product → pre-feasibility → feasibility (techno-economic) → appraisal → DPR.
Social, Technological, Ecological, Economic, Political: the factors in a feasibility study.

front: Objectives of an environmental impact study
back: Identify the environmental resources affected; measure and assess the effects; describe alternatives with different effects.
UNIDO values benefits at shadow (efficiency) prices. L–M classes inputs and outputs as traded, non-traded and labour.
Time to recover the investment from net returns. Ignores returns after pay-back and the time value of money.
$PV = C_n/(1+d)^n$: Rs 100 next year at 10% is worth Rs 90.91 now.
$NPV = B - C$ (accept if > 0); $BCR = B/C$ (accept if > 1); IRR = discount rate at which $NPV = 0$.
Risk: adverse outcome, quantifiable, analysed by probability. Uncertainty: unpredictable, assessed by sensitivity analysis.
A circle on a Gantt bar marking completion of a phase of a task (an event).
PERT: US Navy Polaris, probabilistic (3 estimates), scheduling. CPM: Du Pont, deterministic (1 estimate), time–cost optimisation.
AOA: arrow = activity, circle = event. AON: box = activity, arrow = sequence (used by software).
Burst: more than one activity starts from it. Merge: reached only when more than one activity is complete.
The longest path through the network; its length is the shortest possible project duration. Its activities have zero float.
Forward: EST, start at 0, add durations, take the maximum at merges. Backward: LST, start at the end EST, subtract, take the minimum at bursts.
$TF = L_j - E_i - t$; $FF = E_j - E_i - t$; $IF = E_j - L_i - t$; $TF \ge FF \ge IF$.
Number the initial event 1, delete its outgoing arrows, number the new initial events 2, 3, … until the final event.

front: Five ways to set activity start times
back: Earliest start; latest start; distributing float; arbitrary; by resource availability (the only one that works in practice).
Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
Moving activities within their float so resource demand is as even as possible, without changing the project duration.
$(C_c - C_n)/(T_n - T_c)$: extra cost per unit time saved by crashing.
Crash the critical activity with the least cost slope, only until another path becomes critical; then crash all critical paths together.
Fix review period → obtain progress information → compare with schedule → take corrective action → report; update the network as needed.
FS (default), SS, FF, SF, each with optional lag or lead.
Shows the baseline bar under the scheduled or actual bar, so slippage is visible.
Right place, price, quality, quantity and time.
Requirements planning → solicitation → award → contract administration.
RFQ: informal, price and delivery. RFP: detailed, negotiated, price not primary. ITT: formal, high value, opened publicly.
1) Appoint the supplier early, before final design, on a limited contract. 2) Agree a fixed price and issue the full contract once specifications are final.
Cost = the contractor's expenses. Price = cost + profit (fee), the total the client pays.
The cost or price above which the contractor bears all additional costs.
Fee = target fee + contractor share × (target cost − actual cost), within the min/max fee.
Firm fixed price (most risk on contractor) → FPIF → CPIF → CPFF → cost plus % / T&M (most risk on client).
